engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening: Italian Game Basics
chess.body: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. White targets f7, the weakest square in Black's position. Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5) leads to rich middlegame. Learn: castle early, play d3, develop bishop to e3, then push d4 for centre control. Safe, instructive, good for learning. Magnus Carlsen played this at the top level.

Break the patterns you don't want to pass on. Keep the ones that built you. Each generation improves a little. That's legacy.

book.author: Jim Collins & Jerry Porras
book.lesson: Collins and Porras studied 18 visionary companies (3M, P&G, Disney, HP) against comparison companies over 100 years. The visionary companies were not more focused on profit — they were more focused on a core ideology (core values + purpose) that never changed. But within that fixed core, they drove relentless change in strategy, tactics, products, and people. The paradox: the companies most resistant to changing their values were the most agile in changing everything else. The core ideology acted as an anchor, giving the freedom to experiment. Companies that change their values with market fashion have no anchor and drift.
book.key_quote: Know what must never change (your values and purpose). Change everything else constantly.
book.action: Write your 3 non-negotiable core values. For each, ask: does my current work reflect this? Would I keep this value even if it cost me money?
crux: Visionary companies are built to outlast any single leader, product, or idea.
Be a clock builder, not a time teller. Build the organisation, not the one great idea.
The genius of AND rejects the tyranny of OR — purpose AND profit, stability AND change.
Preserve the core, stimulate progress. The core ideology is fixed; everything else is negotiable.
Core ideology = core values + purpose. It is discovered, not written by committee.
BHAGs — big hairy audacious goals — with a 10 to 30-year horizon.
Cult-like cultures: intense indoctrination, tight fit, elitism. You either belong or you leave.
Try a lot of stuff and keep what works. Evolutionary progress, not just planned strategy.
Home-grown management preserves the core across generations. Outside saviours break it.
Good enough never is. Continuous self-improvement is institutionalised, not motivational.
Great companies are not started by charismatic visionaries with a great idea — often the opposite.
Alignment is the work: every practice must reinforce the ideology or it erodes it.
learnings: Build the machine that produces outcomes, not the outcome.
Refusing the trade-off is often the more interesting option.
Values only count when they cost you something.
Continuity of the core is what allows aggressive change everywhere else.
examples: 3M's 15% time and 'sell no new products' discipline produced Post-it Notes through evolutionary trial, not strategy.
HP kept its core people-first ideology across decades of complete product reinvention, from oscillators to printers.
Boeing bet the company on the 707 and again on the 747 — BHAGs that could have ended it.
adapt: Core ideology for the brand: numbers first, no filler, no fake certainty. That does not change with platform.
BHAG: AED 30K/month by mid-2026 and a self-running product stack. Both dated, both audacious.
Preserve the core, change the channel — the Meta restriction changes distribution, not the voice.
Build the newspaper so it publishes without you. Clock, not time.

interview_tech.q: Model the impact of a 10% AED appreciation on a UAE retailer sourcing from China.
interview_tech.a: Buying gets cheaper in AED terms, so landed cost falls and gross margin expands — but only after existing stock at old cost clears, so the benefit lags by roughly one inventory turn. If the AED is pegged to the USD, the real question is USD/CNY, not AED specifically. On the revenue side, a stronger currency makes the destination more expensive for tourists, which matters in Dubai where tourist spend is a meaningful share of mall retail. Net effect is usually positive on margin, mildly negative on footfall.

interview_tech.q: A supplier offers 5% discount for payment in 10 days instead of 60. Take it?
interview_tech.a: Annualise it. You forgo 5% to accelerate payment by 50 days. The implied annual cost of not taking it is roughly 5/95 × 365/50 ≈ 38%. Unless your marginal cost of capital exceeds 38%, take the discount — this is one of the highest-return decisions in working capital. The caveat is liquidity: if taking it forces you onto an overdraft at 9% you still win, but if it breaches a covenant or leaves no buffer, the arithmetic is not the whole answer.

interview_soft.q: How would your team describe your management style?
interview_soft.a: Answer with evidence rather than adjectives. 'They would say I am specific — I give the number I expect and the date, and I do not change it quietly. They would also say I go into detail on their work more than some managers, which is useful when they are learning and irritating when they are not, so I have had to learn where to stop.' Naming the downside of your own style is what makes the strength believable.

interview_soft.q: How do you handle stress and long hours during close or audit?
interview_soft.a: They are checking sustainability, not stoicism. Do not claim you thrive on pressure. Give the operating answer: what you do to make the peak smaller (moving work out of the close), how you protect the team (rotating the worst shifts, protecting recovery time after), and what you personally do that is non-negotiable. Having a young child is relevant here and worth saying — it reads as someone with real boundaries rather than someone who has not been tested yet.

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: after 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 Bb4, avoid 5...c5?; instead play 5...Nbd7, then …0‑0, …c6, …Re8, keeping the king shielded and preventing premature pawn breaks.
Focus on early piece development: after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6, prioritize Nf3, Nc3, and Bf4 before pushing e‑pawns; you wasted ~3 seconds per move and lost ~0.3 cp.
Focus on early king safety: after 6...e6, avoid 7.Qb3? and instead develop knights (Nf3, Bd3) before queen excursions—prevents the forced queen‑trade loss at move 22.

lichess_summary.session_summary: **Verdict:** Your 33 % win rate shows you’re barely scraping past the median; the opening you use most—*the Italian Game*—is being neutralised by opponents who know the critical 3.Nf3‑d3 line, so you’re handing them a free equaliser every time. Switch immediately to a less predictable, high‑impact system (e.g., the King’s Indian Attack or a solid 1…c5‑based repertoire) and drill the first 10‑12 moves until they become second nature. Stop “thinking” in the middle game; instead, pre‑plan concrete tactical motifs for each opening line and practice them daily with a timer—if you can’t execute a forced sequence under 30 seconds, you’ll never convert the opening advantage into a win.

lichess_puzzle.tip: King activity and pawn structure dominate. Technique over tactics here.
